title: Corey Kispert on NBA Expansion: "I Really Hope They Choose Seattle"
htmlContent:
Corey Kispert plays his basketball in Atlanta now, but his heart is still in the Pacific Northwest. The Atlanta Hawks guard, who grew up in Edmonds, Washington, just north of Seattle, is keeping a close eye on the NBA's expansion plans. Like a lot of people back home, he is nervous that Seattle's long-awaited return to the league is no longer a sure thing.

Seattle Is No Longer a Lock

For years, Seattle and Las Vegas have been seen as the clear front-runners whenever the NBA decided to add two teams. That picture got more complicated in October, when ESPN's Brian Windhorst reported that Commissioner Adam Silver told owners at a Board of Governors meeting that a Seattle franchise was no longer a lock. Silver also floated Mexico City as a possible expansion market, where an ownership group has proposed a team and a new arena district.

Money appears to be a big part of the story. Reports say the leading Seattle group, headed by Kraken co-owner Samantha Holloway, has offered around $6 billion, while bidding in Las Vegas could push the expansion fee as high as $10 billion.

Kispert Sees Leverage at Play

Kispert believes that is exactly what is happening.

"I think they're probably using it as leverage, but they're talking about Oklahoma, Mexico City as an option over Seattle right now. I'm assuming it might be for leverage purposes. It's not a lock that they'll get the expansion." — Corey Kispert

His mention of Oklahoma will sting for Sonics fans. The SuperSonicsleft Seattle in 2008 and became the Oklahoma City Thunder, a move that still hurts in the city. The idea of Seattle losing out again, even in a negotiation, is the kind of thing that makes fans uneasy.

"I Have That Bias"

Kispert didn't pretend to be neutral.

"I sure hope so. Obviously, I'm from Seattle, and so I have that bias. I want to see a team there." — Corey Kispert

He made the case that a team in Seattle would be good for everyone involved.

"I think it'd be good for the league, good for players. Players like the city. And it'd be good for the fans too." — Corey Kispert

That point about players matters. Seattle has a strong basketball reputation. The region has produced NBA talent for decades, and players often talk about enjoying visits to the city. Climate Pledge Arena, home of the NHL's Kraken, already exists and is ready to host an NBA team. For a league weighing new markets, that is a strong selling point.

A Long Wait for Sonics Fans

"They've been starving for a team for what, 16, 17 years now?" — Corey Kispert tells LandonBuford.com

It has actually been even longer. The Sonics played their last game in Seattle in 2008, which means fans have gone 18 years without NBA basketball. In that time, they have kept the green and gold alive with packed preseason games, throwback jerseys and constant pressure on the league to return.

From Edmonds to the NBA

Kispert's connection to the area is real. He grew up in the Seattle area before becoming a star at Gonzaga, where he was a key part of a team that reached the national championship game in 2021. He was drafted by Washington that summer and spent several seasons with the Wizards before Atlanta acquired him in January 2026in the trade that sent Trae Young to Washington.

He is one of many NBA players with Pacific Northwest roots who would love a home crowd in Seattle.

Out of His Hands

"So yeah, I really hope they choose Seattle. I got nothing to do with that, but I hope they do." — Corey Kispert

The decision belongs to Silver and the owners, and the timeline remains uncertain. League officials had suggested expansion news could come before the end of the year, but negotiations over price could slow things down.

Until then, Seattle fans will keep waiting and hoping. They have at least one NBA player firmly on their side.
excerpt: Atlanta Hawks guard Corey Kispert, who grew up in Edmonds, Washington, says he hopes Seattle lands an NBA expansion team, acknowledging his hometown bias while making the case that a franchise there would be good for the league, players, and fans alike.
